subject: What is mlik really equal to?

messages.author: f31345e547589d21
messages.subject: What is mlik really equal to?
parts:
Hi,

What is mlik really equal to ?
Reasons for this silly question are :
  1. mlik stands for marginal likelihood. But its value is given on log scale. Hence, it is actually the log marginal likelihood ; 
  2. In the R-dlm package, the function dlmLL is described as "Function that computes the log likelihood of a state space model." but the value is defined as "The function returns the negative of the loglikelihood" ;
  3. With R-dlm, I'm estimating nested models by iteratively adding parameters e.g. for taking into account appropriately outliers (i.e. nor false or doubtful data, but really exceptional) ; mechanically, the log-likelihoods of these models increase;
  4. With R-INLA, I'm doing the same thing, but the mlik (on a log scale) are decreasing.
I'm taking outliers into account as describe here :
https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/c3-MyeIijFE/m/k8fp62FfAgAJ
Thanks in advance
Regards
DS

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What is mlik really equal to?
parts:
Hi,
When you say in point 3 that “mechanically, the log-likelihoods of these models increase “ I think you’re mistaken. The marginal “likelihood” in the Bayesian setting is the joint pdf/pmf for observations and unknowns integrated over the unknowns,
p(y) = int  p(y,theta) d\theta = int p(y|theta) p(theta) d\theta
When you you expand the model with more parameters, you’re increasing the flexibility of the model to generate different data, and unless the priors are changed in certain ways as well, you’re likely to end up with a smaller value for p(y), as your particular observation is less probable in the expanded model.

In frequentist settings, one instead commonly considers the maximum likelihood value instead, which can have a very different behaviour to the integrated likelihood.

(Also, the marginal likelihood isn’t actually a likelihood; the likelihood is the observation density seen as a function of the parameters, which isn’t the same thing as the joint, conditional, or marginal densities. I’m not sure who started using this misleading terminology in the Bayesian literature, but unfortunately it seems we have to live with it…)

Finn
